whyItMatters: Transforms the economy again: new industries, new technologies, new forms of corporate organization. Germany's industrial rise directly contributes to great-power rivalries and WWI.
causes: Scientific advances applied to industry; New energy sources (electricity, petroleum); Corporate organization and finance; Government investment in infrastructure and education
effects: Mass production and consumer goods; New industrial powers (Germany, US); Urbanization accelerates; Working-class grows; Intensified international competition; Foundation for total war capability
memoryHook: 2nd Industrial Rev: steel, chemicals, electricity — Germany rises, Britain worries

title: Decolonization
description: European colonial empires dissolve as colonies gain independence — sometimes peacefully (British India), sometimes violently (Algeria, Vietnam).
whyItMatters: Ends 500 years of European global dominance. Shows how WWII weakened imperial powers and how anti-colonial nationalism drew on European revolutionary ideas.
causes: WWII weakens European powers; Anti-colonial nationalism; Cold War context (US/USSR oppose colonialism); UN Charter supports self-determination; Cost of maintaining empires
effects: Dozens of new nations in Africa and Asia; Algerian War (1954-62) traumatizes France; Suez Crisis (1956) humiliates Britain and France; Immigration to former colonial powers; Postcolonial identities and conflicts
memoryHook: Decolonization: empires built over 500 years crumble in 30

title: Welfare State
description: Western European governments build comprehensive social safety nets: national health care, pensions, unemployment insurance, public education — the 'cradle to grave' welfare state.
whyItMatters: Defines post-war Western European society. Shows how capitalism was reformed (not replaced) to prevent the conditions that produced fascism and communism.
causes: Post-war consensus for social reform; Beveridge Report (1942) in Britain; Fear of return to Depression-era conditions; Labor/social democratic political strength; Cold War competition with communist welfare claims
effects: Universal healthcare (NHS in Britain); Comprehensive social insurance; Reduced inequality; Consumer society; Later challenged by neoliberalism (Thatcher, 1980s)
memoryHook: Welfare state: from cradle to grave — government provides, capitalism persists

title: Bacon and Descartes: New Methods
description: Francis Bacon promotes empiricism/inductive reasoning; René Descartes promotes rationalism/deductive reasoning — together they establish the foundations of modern scientific method.
whyItMatters: Bacon and Descartes define the two pillars of modern knowledge: observation and reason. Essential for understanding how the Scientific Revolution changes European thought.
causes: Scientific Revolution demands new methods; Dissatisfaction with Aristotelian/scholastic methods; Renaissance emphasis on observation
effects: Empiricism influences British philosophical tradition (Locke, Hume); Rationalism influences continental philosophy; Scientific method combining both approaches; Foundation for Enlightenment epistemology
memoryHook: Bacon = observe the world; Descartes = 'I think, therefore I am'

title: Voltaire and Religious Toleration
description: Voltaire champions religious toleration, free speech, and rational critique of superstition and fanaticism, becoming the Enlightenment's most famous voice.
whyItMatters: Voltaire embodies the Enlightenment attack on intolerance and institutional religion. His wit and prolific writing make him the go-to example for Enlightenment critique.
causes: Exposure to English liberty and Locke during exile; Outrage at religious persecution (Calas affair); Enlightenment values of reason and toleration
effects: Popularizes Enlightenment ideas across Europe; Attacks on Catholic Church influence anticlerical movements; 'Écrasez l'infâme' (crush the infamous thing); Model for public intellectual engagement
memoryHook: Voltaire: 'I may not agree with what you say, but I will defend your right to say it'

title: Napoleonic Code
description: Napoleon's comprehensive legal code establishes legal equality, property rights, and secular authority — codifying key revolutionary principles while reinforcing patriarchal authority.
whyItMatters: Outlasts Napoleon's empire: adopted across Europe and beyond. Represents both the Revolution's achievements (legal equality) and limits (women's subordination).
causes: Need to unify France's varied legal systems; Revolutionary principles of equality before law; Napoleon's desire for efficient administration
effects: Legal equality and property rights codified; Spread across conquered territories; Patriarchal family law (women subordinated); Model for legal systems worldwide; Enduring legacy in continental European law
memoryHook: Napoleonic Code: equality before law (for men); women wait

title: Agricultural Revolution
description: Innovations in farming (crop rotation, enclosure, selective breeding, seed drill) increase food production, support population growth, and free labor for factories.
whyItMatters: Precondition for Industrial Revolution: more food → population growth → surplus labor → factory workers. Enclosure displaces peasants, creating the industrial workforce.
causes: Scientific approach to farming; Enclosure movement consolidates land; New crops from Columbian Exchange; Market incentives for efficiency
effects: Population growth; Peasants displaced by enclosure → move to cities; Surplus labor for factories; Foundation for Industrial Revolution
memoryHook: Agri Revolution: better farming → more people → workers for factories

title: Seven Years' War
region: France; Britain; Austria; German States; Russia
description: Global conflict ('first world war') pitting Britain/Prussia against France/Austria/Russia; Britain gains French colonies, Prussia survives, France is weakened financially.
whyItMatters: Reshapes the colonial balance (Britain dominates) and weakens France financially — a direct cause of the French Revolution's fiscal crisis.
causes: Diplomatic Revolution (alliance shift); Colonial rivalry between Britain and France; Prussian-Austrian rivalry; Frederick II's aggression
effects: British colonial supremacy (Treaty of Paris 1763); French financial crisis → contributes to Revolution; Prussia confirmed as great power; Diplomatic Revolution pattern
memoryHook: Seven Years' War: Britain wins colonies, France goes broke → Revolution

title: Feminism and Women's Rights Movements
description: Women organize for legal rights, education, property ownership, and eventually suffrage; Mary Wollstonecraft, suffragettes, and feminist intellectuals challenge patriarchy.
whyItMatters: Essential AP social history: shows how excluded groups use Enlightenment and revolutionary language to demand inclusion. Key for gender-themed essays and complexity points.
causes: Enlightenment ideas of natural rights applied to women; Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792); Women's role in revolutions and reform movements; Industrialization changes women's economic roles
effects: Property rights for married women; Access to education and professions; Suffragette movement (early 20th century); Limited suffrage gains before WWI; WWI accelerates women's suffrage
memoryHook: Wollstonecraft: 'If women have reason, they deserve rights' → suffragettes follow

title: Munich Agreement (Appeasement)
description: Britain and France allow Hitler to annex the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia in exchange for 'peace in our time' — appeasement's most notorious failure.
whyItMatters: Defines the concept of appeasement. Chamberlain's failure to stop Hitler at Munich becomes the cautionary tale for all subsequent foreign policy. Key for causation of WWII.
causes: Hitler's demand for Sudetenland (German speakers); British/French desire to avoid war; Memories of WWI carnage; Belief that Hitler's demands were limited
effects: Hitler emboldened — takes rest of Czechoslovakia (1939); Appeasement discredited; War becomes inevitable; Churchill vindicated; Lesson shapes Cold War resolve
memoryHook: Munich 1938: Chamberlain waves paper, says 'peace' — wrong

title: Berlin Wall Built
description: East Germany builds a wall dividing Berlin to stop mass emigration to the West — becomes the most potent symbol of Cold War division.
whyItMatters: Physical embodiment of the Iron Curtain. Its fall in 1989 becomes the symbol of communism's collapse. Essential evidence for Cold War essays.
causes: Mass emigration from East to West Germany; Soviet desire to stabilize East German regime; Cold War tensions over Berlin
effects: Families divided; East Germany stabilized (temporarily); Symbol of Cold War oppression; Its fall (1989) becomes the defining image of communism's end
memoryHook: 1961: wall goes up, divides Berlin; 1989: wall comes down, Europe reunites
